##### Chokepoint disruptions and their macroeconomic consequences

Key takeaways

• Rising geopolitical tensions, including trade restrictions and conflicts, are increasingly disrupting global supply chains, posing significant risks at critical chokepoints. 
• Strong substitution effects and the use of inventories have helped to mitigate adverse output effects of chokepoint disruptions, but they often come at the cost of higher input prices. 
• An effective policy response to chokepoint disruptions requires a tailored approach that takes account of the cause, centrality and the private sector’s ability to substitute and draw on buffers. 
The Covid-19 pandemic, the rising use of trade restrictions and the recent disruptions around the Strait of 
Hormuz have exposed weaknesses in global supply chains. When shocks hit critical links – chokepoints 
with limited substitutability – the effects can propagate well beyond the firms and the countries directly 
affected. This Bulletin documents these chokepoints, assesses how their disruption affects the 
macroeconomy and draws policy implications. 
On average, disruptions at chokepoints are associated with larger output losses and stronger price 
pressures than comparable disruptions elsewhere. Yet the realised impact in any episode depends on the 
affected product and available adjustment margins, including the ease of substitution, inventory buffers 
and pricing margins. 
The policy prescription to look through first-round effects on inflation remains appropriate as long as 
the risk of inflation expectations de-anchoring stays low. However, policy calibration might have to 
consider the disruption’s position and centrality in the supply chain, the ease of substitution, the state of 
buffers (inventories, spare capacity, margins) and demand. 

Geopolitical tensions bring chokepoints into focus

Geopolitical factors are playing an increasingly prominent role in driving supply chain disruptions. This trend is evident in firms’ earnings calls, which highlight the rising incidence of geopolitically driven disruptions, alongside a renewed surge in logistics concerns that had previously spiked during the pandemic (Graph 1.A). These developments have drawn fresh attention to the critical vulnerabilities posed by chokepoints in global supply chains. A supply chain chokepoint is an economically important product or node – such as a firm, industry in a country, production location or transport route – for which substitutes are limited or cannot be activated quickly. While a disruption to an ordinary node may be temporary and localised, a disruption to a chokepoint can spread more broadly through production networks. Its economic importance may stem from the direct use of an output across many sectors, as with refined oil products, or from significant indirect effects through supply chain connections, as with semiconductors, which are critical inputs for industries as diverse as automotive manufacturing and modern food production.

A key form of chokepoint arises from production network centrality – when nodes lie on numerous production paths, making them critical to the functioning of global supply chains. Many of these nodes are concentrated in large economies and in manufacturing sectors (Graph 1.B). Notable examples include German machinery manufacturing, Chinese manufacturing of electrical machinery and fertiliser production in the Middle East, all of which have become more central over time.

The severity of a disruption at a chokepoint depends not only on its centrality but also on how readily firms can find alternatives. The most direct form of substitution involves sourcing the same product from other suppliers. Estimated trade elasticities – which measure how strongly trade flows respond when relative prices change – shed light on this form of substitution. Comparing these elasticities with world trade shares – a proxy for economic importance – reveals significant differences across goods (Graph 1.C).

Mining and energy-related products combine a large trade share with relatively high substitutability across suppliers. By contrast, electronic products, including semiconductors, are both economically critical and more difficult to source elsewhere. Basic metals, which include some rare earth elements, are also hard to substitute, although they account for a lower share of international trade. The scope for substitution also depends on how concentrated production is. In particular, alternatives may be limited or difficult to access quickly when supply is concentrated in a few countries. From this perspective, the steady rise in the export concentration of intermediate inputs across countries over the past three decades points to declining substitutability and greater exposure to chokepoints (Graph 2.A). Part of this increasing concentration reflects the adaptation of trade and production networks around a small number of processing hubs. In electrification metals, for instance, supply chains have increasingly taken a hub-and-spoke form centred on China, thanks to a combination of sustained investment and industrial policy measures (Kirk et al (2026); Banerjee et al (2026)).

Macroeconomic implications 
Evidence confirms that chokepoint disruptions have a quantitatively significant effect on economic activity 
and prices. For instance, a one standard deviation increase in disruptions at key country-sector nodes1 of 
the global supply network is associated with a 50% larger decline in global industrial production growth 
compared with an equally large disruption at less critical nodes (Graph 2.B). Moreover, within one year 
disruptions at key nodes also raise downstream firms’ producer prices by about 70 basis points, while 
those at less important nodes have minimal impact (Graph 2.C). 
Additional analysis indicates how the size of these effects depends on multiple factors, including the 
nature of the disruption, the scope for substitution, inventory levels and margins, among others. As to the 
nature of the disruption, earnings call data indicate that firms are more likely to seek substitutes and 
reallocate production in response to trade restrictions and other geopolitical disruptions than to natural 
disasters or health crises, presumably because the former are expected to be more persistent (Graph 3.A). 
By contrast, logistical disruptions typically prompt like-for-like sourcing from alternative suppliers rather 
than broader adjustments.
